title: Make your own prompt templates
summary: Save prompts that work and fill in the blanks next time

steps.body:
When a prompt works well, **don't throw it away**. Save it to reuse — in LINE Keep or your phone's notes app.

How to make a template:
1. Take a prompt that gave you a good result
2. Find the parts that **change every time** and put them in [square brackets], like [product name] or [price]
3. Give it a name you'll remember, like “Sales post” or “Reply to review”

Next time, just copy it, fill in the brackets and send.

Important: **the parts that stay the same** — length, tone, format — are what make the prompt good. Don't cut them.

steps.prompt:
Template “Sales post”:
I run a [type of shop] in [area]. Write a Facebook post selling [product name] for [price] baht. What makes it special: [selling point]. Max 4 lines, casual tone, 2–3 emojis, and end by inviting people to message me on LINE.

This time:
[type of shop] = Thai dessert shop
[area] = Lat Phrao
[product name] = mango sticky rice
[price] = 60
[selling point] = sweet, juicy Nam Dok Mai mangoes, sticky rice made fresh every morning
steps.output:
Mango sticky rice is here 🥭
Sweet, juicy Nam Dok Mai mangoes + sticky rice made fresh every morning
Just 60 baht a box — ordering open around Lat Phrao
Message us on LINE to reserve before it sells out 💬✨
steps.note: The weak template only keeps a blank and loses everything that made the prompt good (length, tone, ending). The good one keeps it all and only swaps what's in the brackets.

steps.question:
To turn this prompt into a template, which part belongs in brackets?
“Write a LINE message telling Mr. Somchai his parcel arrives on Friday. Polite tone, max 3 lines.”
options: The customer's name and the delivery day
steps.explain: The name and day change every time, so they become [customer name] and [delivery day]. The tone and length are what you want every time, so they stay.

steps.task:
Create a prompt template you'd use often — for example, replying to customer reviews, writing a leave request or summarizing a meeting.

Use [square brackets] for the parts that change each time.
rubric: Bracket names make it clear what to fill in (e.g. [customer name], not [xxx])
The fixed parts include good-prompt elements such as context, length or format, and tone
Truly reusable: no one-time details hard-coded where a bracket should be
steps.placeholder: e.g. Reply to a review from [customer name] who wrote: [review text]...
